results.title: Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s disease: pathogenic signaling, biomarkers, and emerging therapeutic interventions
results.summary: <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia worldwide, characterized by progressive cognitive decline and neurodegeneration. Although amyloid-β plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau are major pathological hallmarks, increasing evidence highlights persistent neuroinflammation as a critical contributor to disease progression. Activated microglia and astrocytes, inflammatory cytokines, inflammasome activation, and dysregulated immune responses promote neuronal damage and synaptic dysfunction. Similar inflammatory mechanisms are observed in neurological disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and brain tumors, suggesting shared molecular pathways linking neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and tumor-associated immune responses. Proteomics, transcriptomics, and multi-omics approaches provide powerful strategies to characterize disease-associated molecular signatures, signaling pathways, biomarkers, and therapeutic targets. This review summarizes key neuroinflammatory mechanisms in AD, including NF-κB, NLRP3, PI3K/Akt, MAPK, cGAS–STING, mitochondrial, lysosomal, calcium, insulin, and blood–brain barrier pathways. Recent advances in proteomic and transcriptomic profiling and their integration with genomic, epigenomic, and metabolomic data are discussed for understanding disease heterogeneity and identifying clinically relevant biomarkers. Current and emerging therapeutic strategies, including anti-Aβ antibodies, anti-inflammatory agents, selective inhibitors, dual-target compounds, PROTACs, and protein–protein interaction modulators, are also evaluated. Finally, multi-omics-based precision medicine and artificial intelligence-assisted analysis may facilitate biomarker-guided patient stratification and development of effective disease-modifying therapies.</jats:p>

results.title: A four-gene diagnostic panel for distinguishing primary progressive multiple sclerosis from HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis
results.summary:
J Neuroimmunol. 2026 Nov 3;423:579120. doi: 10.1016/j.jneuroim.2026.579120. Online ahead of print.

ABSTRACT

Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis (PPMS) and HTLV-1-Associated Myelopathy/Tropical Spastic Paraparesis (HAM/TSP) are clinically overlapping progressive myelopathies characterized by spastic paraparesis and autonomic dysfunction. However, they originate from fundamentally distinct pathogenic processes: autoimmune demyelination in PPMS versus chronic retroviral-driven neuroinflammation in HAM/TSP. Current diagnostic approaches are frequently inadequate, as HTLV-1 screening is often omitted in non-endemic regions and positive serology in endemic areas does not rule out concomitant PPMS, highlighting the urgent need for complementary molecular diagnostic tools. In this study, we developed an integrative bioinformatics framework combining network analysis, differential expression profiling, and machine learning to identify a transcriptional signature capable of distinguishing PPMS from HAM/TSP. Disease-specific gene modules were identified through cross-dataset preservation analysis and module-trait correlations. Random Forest classification with recursive feature elimination was employed to derive a parsimonious Diagnostic Risk Score (DRS), which was validated on an independent external cohort under a frozen-threshold, leakage-free design. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) revealed striking topological divergence between the two diseases: HAM/TSP exhibited a consolidated network architecture with a single dominant module, whereas PPMS displayed a highly fragmented topology with numerous smaller modules. Cross-dataset preservation analysis identified 11 PPMS-specific and 63 HAM/TSP-specific candidate biomarker genes. Machine learning refinement reduced this to a 4-gene signature comprising ZFAND1, MAPRE2, TBK1, and LPAR6, which achieved robust classification performance in cross-validation (macro-averaged accuracy: 0.982; macro-averaged F1-score: 0.987; AUC-ROC: 0.995) and robust performance on external validation (macro-averaged accuracy: 0.975; macro-averaged F1-score: 0.937; AUC-ROC: 0.800). The 4-gene signature captures distinct biological dimensions: ZFAND1 marks proteostatic stress from viral inflammation, TBK1 excludes the HTLV-1 interferon signature, MAPRE2 reflects a HAM/TSP-associated cytoskeletal program, and LPAR6 links inflammatory signaling to oligodendrocyte maturation. This multidimensional architecture explains the panel's high accuracy and offers mechanistic insights. The proposed approach offers a practical, transcriptome-based adjunct to current diagnostic methods, with potential to guide therapeutic stratification and reduce misdiagnosis of PPMS and HAM/TSP.

results.title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation
results.summary:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, clinical text, and digitally measured behavior, but reported performance often exceeds the maturity of clinical evidence.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Method</jats:title>
<jats:p>We conducted a structured narrative review, informed by SANRA principles, of English‐language human studies, reviews, and regulatory sources identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore from January 2022 through July 2026; older landmark studies were retained when necessary for historical or methodological context. We applied a common translational‐evidence framework across six prespecified neurological domains to distinguish technical performance from external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, implementation, and demonstrated patient benefit. Evidence was appraised according to cohort representativeness, patient‐level data separation, external and prospective validation, calibration, clinical comparators, regulatory status, workflow integration, and patient‐level benefit.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Finding</jats:title>
<jats:p>Across stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and neuro‐oncology, the strongest evidence concerns narrowly defined imaging and signal‐processing tasks. A cluster‐randomized stroke study demonstrated shorter thrombectomy workflow time, and several externally validated models show improved portability. In contrast, many high‐accuracy classification and segmentation studies remain retrospective, single‐dataset, internally validated, and uncalibrated. Multimodal learning, foundation models, federated learning, and large language models broaden capability but introduce additional risks related to dataset shift, bias, opacity, privacy, and automation.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
<jats:p>Neuro‐AI should be judged by its intended clinical task and evidence maturity rather than headline accuracy. Multicenter external validation, prospective workflow evaluation, calibration, subgroup reporting, human‐factors testing, and post‐deployment surveillance are prerequisites for safe and equitable clinical use.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Automated optic chiasm segmentation in magnetic resonance imaging of multiple sclerosis patients using a multi-view, multi-class U-Net with limited annotated data
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Accurate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based segmentation of the optic chiasm is essential for the quantitative assessment of visual pathway damage in multiple sclerosis (MS). However, accurate segmentation remains challenging because of the structure’s small size, complex anatomy, and marked foreground–background imbalance. Existing deep learning approaches often rely on single-view imaging and may not fully exploit complementary anatomical information across MRI planes. To address these limitations, we developed and evaluated a novel multi-view two-dimensional U-Net (2D U-Net) framework that jointly leverages axial and coronal MRI information within a unified segmentation architecture for automated optic chiasm segmentation.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Materials and Methods:</jats:title>
<jats:p>In this secondary analysis, a novel multi-view 2D U-Net framework was developed for optic chiasm segmentation by integrating axial and coronal MRI images within a unified three-class segmentation architecture. Models were optimized using a Tversky loss function and evaluated using five-fold patient-wise cross-validation. Segmentation performance was assessed quantitatively using multiple metrics, with the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), intersection over union (IoU), and balanced accuracy serving as the primary evaluation metrics, and qualitatively through visual comparison with expert annotations.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
<jats:p>A total of 58 patients with relapsing-remitting MS were included in the analysis. The proposed multi-view model demonstrated stable convergence and achieved the highest segmentation performance among all evaluated models, with a DSC of 91.28%, IoU of 84.05%, and balanced accuracy of 94.43%. Compared with the best-performing single-view model, the multi-view approach improved DSC and IoU by approximately 13 and 19 percentage points, respectively. Qualitative assessment showed closer agreement between multi-view segmentations and expert annotations.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
<jats:p>The proposed multi-view, multi-class 2D U-Net framework outperformed conventional single-view models for optic chiasm segmentation. These findings demonstrate that integrating complementary anatomical information from axial and coronal MRI planes can substantially improve segmentation performance. The results indicate the potential of multi-view learning for the automated segmentation of small and anatomically complex structures.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Feasibility of applying generative AI to create managed care pharmacy formulary reviews
results.summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>Formulary reviews are used with other data sources and clinical judgement to support formulary strategies, such as placement for existing and new-to-market drugs. We describe the pharmacy resident user experience and assessed the feasibility of using clinical and research-focused generative artificial (genAI) tools in a managed care setting for creating formulary reviews for 2 complex and rare diseases: multiple sclerosis and age-related macular degeneration. This allowed genAI feasibility assessment for disease states with less well-defined guidelines and fewer data sources from which to draw information.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
<jats:p>Users reported a steeper learning curve with research-specific genAI systems compared with pharmacy-focused tools. Users noted pharmacy-focused genAI tools may produce more current drug pipeline information, relative to research-focused AI systems. Prompt engineering, the skill of creating effective prompts to elicit accurate information from genAI models, also contributed to the quality of the evidence produced, regardless of the tool used. The pharmacists noted time savings when utilizing AI compared with a completely manual data generation process involving individual searches of PubMed, business reports, FDA websites, and pharmaceutical company-related information sources.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
<jats:p>Pharmacists need adequate time and training to optimize prompt techniques to produce quality health- and medication-related information and must be educated on potential downsides of genAI such as inaccurate or incomplete results. With currently available tools, all generated output required careful human fact checking. With continued use and accumulating experience, the pharmacist may become more efficient over time with genAI support for formulary reviews</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Artificial intelligence–based voice biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of neurological diseases: current evidence, limitations, and clinical perspectives
results.summary:
Comput Biol Med. 2026 Nov 4;218:112041. doi: 10.1016/j.compbiomed.2026.112041. Online ahead of print.

ABSTRACT

BACKGROUND: Early diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of neurological diseases remain major clinical challenges because current diagnostic approaches are often expensive, invasive, or insufficiently sensitive to detect early functional changes. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach for analyzing voice and speech as non-invasive digital biomarkers capable of capturing subtle alterations associated with neurological dysfunction.

METHODS: This narrative review analyzed studies published between 2015 and 2026 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The review critically examines the limitations of current neurological diagnostic methods, summarizes the available evidence on AI-based voice and speech biomarkers, discusses machine learning and deep learning approaches applied to speech analysis, and evaluates the methodological, ethical, and regulatory challenges that currently limit their clinical implementation.

RESULTS: Current evidence indicates that AI-based voice biomarkers have considerable potential for screening, diagnostic support, and longitudinal monitoring of neurological disorders, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, and other neurodegenerative conditions. Several studies report high diagnostic performance under controlled experimental settings. However, substantial heterogeneity in study design, sample size, languages, speech acquisition protocols, validation strategies, and reporting standards limits direct comparison between studies and hinders clinical translation. External validation and prospective multicenter studies remain scarce.

CONCLUSION: AI-based voice analysis represents a promising, scalable, and non-invasive complement to conventional neurological assessment, with particular potential for remote screening and disease monitoring. Nevertheless, current evidence does not yet support routine clinical implementation. Future progress will depend on standardized speech acquisition protocols, robust external validation across diverse populations, explainable AI models, and regulatory frameworks capable of ensuring safety, reproducibility, and clinical reliability.

results.title: Spasticity in Multiple Sclerosis: 2026 Expert Consensus
results.summary: <jats:p>Background: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neuroinflammatory disease that significantly impairs quality of life. Spasticity is one of the most frequent and highly disabling features of MS, often accompanied by cramps, pain, bladder dysfunction, sleep disturbances, fatigue, and tremor. Recently, the concept of ‘spasticity-plus syndrome’ (SPS) has emerged to reflect the interplay among these symptoms. This work aims to update the Spanish clinical guideline for managing MS-related spasticity (MSS) by adopting this evolving concept. Methods: A panel of 14 Spanish neurologists assessed the available evidence using a two-level literature review strategy, combining a systematic review focused on SPS with a rapid review of MSS management. Building on the previous guideline, the panel formulated updated recommendations with the scientific endorsement of the Spanish Society of Neurology (SEN). To support a structured and transparent development process, an adapted GRADE-informed framework was used to guide the appraisal of the evidence and formulation of recommendations. Results: A total of nine publications addressing the SPS concept were identified. Based on the evidence and expert consensus, the panel developed 13 recommendations covering triggering and aggravating factors, the diagnosis and evaluation of spasticity, and therapeutic strategies for patient management. In addition, a comprehensive treatment algorithm was proposed to guide therapeutic decision-making according to patients’ clinical profiles. Conclusions: This work provides updated recommendations for the management of patients with MSS, integrating the SPS concept into clinical practice. The panel highlights the importance of a symptom-oriented approach that considers the full spectrum of clinical manifestations to individualize treatment, simplify the therapeutic approach, and minimize the risk of polypharmacy.</jats:p>

results.title: Revisiting the MS paradox: automated 2.5D FLAIR segmentation and DTI microstructural profiling reveals dissociation between lesion burden and reference-like intralesional tract profiles
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
<jats:p>Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals macroscopic lesion burden in multiple sclerosis (MS) but correlates poorly with clinical phenotype, a phenomenon known as the clinico-radiological paradox. While diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics assess microstructural damage, standard whole-lesion averaging may obscure microstructurally spared white matter within heterogeneous plaques.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>We propose a fully automated, multimodal pipeline to identify and quantify reference-like intralesional segments (RLIS) within MS lesions (i.e., the cluster exhibiting maximum feature-space similarity to subject-specific, lesion-spared reference tissue). A modified 2.5D U-Net, developed and evaluated on a cohort of 75 MS patients (115 series), performed automated FLAIR lesion segmentation. In an independent cohort of 100 MS subjects, intralesional DTI metrics (FA and MD) were extracted along streamlines reconstructed via Constrained Spherical Deconvolution tractography. Unsupervised clustering algorithms, validated against a subject-specific, lesion-spared reference CST streamlines (internal capsule), identified operationally defined reference-like segments.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>The 2.5D U-Net achieved robust segmentation performance (DSC: 0.732, VC: 0.954), exhibited higher nominal metrics in a contextual benchmark comparison (DSC: 0.682, VC: 0.864). Across the clinical cohort, lesion count (11–131) and volume (0.54–57.3 mL) varied widely. Among the evaluated clustering methods, K-Means and Gaussian Mixture Models proved to be the most conservative, identifying median reference-like segment proportions of 26% and 22%, respectively. Crucially, the proportion of reference-like intralesional segments showed no significant monotonic association with macroscopic lesion volume or count.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
<jats:p>This automated framework successfully integrates robust deep learning-based lesion segmentation with tract-specific analysis to quantify the proportion of reference-like intralesional segments. The observed dissociation between overall lesion burden and RLIS suggests that this index serves as a promising candidate metric for exploring microstructural features that may contribute to the clinico-radiological paradox.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: A Belgian study assessing relapsing multiple sclerosis activity through automated magnetic resonance imaging volumetry
results.summary:
Neurodegener Dis Manag. 2026 Nov 1:1-13. doi: 10.1080/17582024.2026.2752856. Online ahead of print.

ABSTRACT

AIM: This study assessed to what extent icobrain ms, a commercially available artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) volumetry software, detected disease activity in patients with clinically and radiologically stable relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS), and estimated its impact on radiologists' assessments.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: We retrospectively enrolled 111 RMS patients with two consecutive MRI scans at one year interval, without relapses, progression or radiological changes while remaining on stable therapy. MRI scans were analyzed by four radiologists acting independently, and by icobrain ms. The radiologists performed their assessments both without and with icobrain ms support and categorized patient status based on lesion and brain volume changes.

RESULTS: Radiologists' detection of lesion activity non-significantly increased from 6.8% to 8.6% (McNemar p = 0.215; ordinal regression p = 0.06; sign-test p = 0.08) using icobrain ms. Detection of accelerated brain volume loss increased from 2.0% to 7.7% (all p < 0.01). Inter-reader agreement improved from 36% to 56% for lesions, and from 26% to 40% for brain loss (Kendall's W, p < 0.001). Icobrain ms detected new or significantly enlarged lesions in 16.2% and accelerated brain volume loss in 6.3% of participants.

CONCLUSION: AI-assisted MRI volumetry may support radiologists to detect subclinical disease activity in patients characterized as having stable disease.

results.title: Computational identification of EBNA1-binding candidates using machine learning-based virtual screening and molecular docking
results.summary: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is associated with several malignancies and multiple sclerosis, and Epstein–Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) plays an essential role in viral genome replication and episome maintenance. The experimentally characterized KVD-associated pocket within the EBNA1 DNA-binding domain provides a structurally defined site for computational ligand prioritization. This study aimed to identify and prioritize predicted EBNA1-binding candidates using an integrated machine-learning and structure-based virtual screening framework. A PubChem EBNA1 bioactivity dataset comprising 304,124 records was curated to obtain 4,584 unique compounds. Molecular representation combined 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints with 11 RDKit molecular descriptors. Random Forest, SVM-RBF, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost models were evaluated using scaffold-based independent testing. The optimized XGBoost model was applied to a non-overlapping DrugBank library of 12,287 compounds. Compounds with predicted activity probabilities ≥0.5 were subjected to Lipinski-based filtering, followed by molecular docking against the KVD-associated binding pocket of EBNA1 (PDB ID: 6NPM). Docking validation was performed by independent KVD redocking at exhaustiveness values of 8, 16, and 32. Post-docking candidates were further evaluated using PAINS, aggregation, frequent-hitter/promiscuity, assay-interference, redox-associated structural-alert, and ADMET assessments. XGBoost demonstrated the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.835), PR-AUC (0.408), and best Brier score (0.067), and was selected for virtual screening. Screening identified 116 compounds above the probability threshold, of which 40 satisfied Lipinski criteria and were docked. Thirty-two compounds achieved docking scores ≤ −7.0 kcal/mol. Sequential liability assessment and integrated prioritization identified 10 computationally prioritized EBNA1-binding candidates with favorable combined machine-learning, docking, and structural-filter profiles. The integrated computational framework enabled systematic prioritization of structurally diverse predicted EBNA1-binding candidates for further experimental investigation. The identified candidates represent computationally prioritized molecules for subsequent biochemical and functional evaluation of EBNA1 binding and activity and should not be interpreted as experimentally validated antiviral or disease-modifying agents.
